title: An outlet reports that an Anthropic employee manages a consensual-non-consent party business, and that women in AI feel pressured to attend
claim: The orgies have been the subject of sexual assault allegations and sparked debate about the AI industry's attitudes toward women, some of whom report feeling pressured to attend the orgies in order to advance their careers.

checks.what: Business filing: the 17 Aug 2023 statement of information for Red Means No LLC lists three managers, one of them the Anthropic employee named in the article.
checks.source: California Secretary of State filing, via bizprofile.net

checks.what: “Runs a business”: a March 2026 registry snapshot still lists him as one of two managers. A manager listing does not say who runs the events; the article's own body says he is “listed as a manager”.

The business's rules: its site says its events are “designed to be spaces to both ignore the "nos" of others, and have your own "nos" ignored”, that “By entering and wearing a wristband, you give default consent to all the actions listed”, including “Moderate Spanking”, “Wrestling” and “Light pain (1–5/10)”, with “Light electricity” and “Moderate beatings*” “permitted with negotiation”. The same site says consent is revocable with the word “red”, that “actual consent violations are strictly forbidden”, that entry is by application, and that attendees sign a consent form and waiver. No public complaint process is described.
checks.source: the business's own website (named, not linked)

checks.what: An assault account: a first-person post (24 Feb 2025, the last of a three-part series) describes her first Red Means No party: a participant “ignored the default consent rules, fucking multiple women without protection”. She calls it “a form of sexual assault”, writes that she was “actually sexually assaulted at my first CNC party”, and calls him “the stealther”. It says the organizers “kicked the stealther out of the party, made him submit additional follow-up STI tests”, “banned him from future parties, and reported the incident to other party organizers in the area”, and “wrote up an in depth incident report”. The post does not say whether the incident was reported to the police. It also says “The support I received from my new poly community was revelatory.” No account of another incident was found.
checks.source: the author's own post on Substack (a private person, not named here); the Free Beacon article links to it

checks.what: Career pressure: the article gives it to unnamed women and critics, and quotes three named commentators (below). The post it quotes says “There are some who are contesting the assertion that it functions as an AI networking event”. A third party's post on X shown there quotes the researcher as “I personally do upgrade my assessment of someone's AI alignment qualifications if I find out they go to [Red Means No]” (his own comment reads “absolutely do upgrade”) and “there are many other signals which can substitute for it.”

The cofounder's own account (Feb 2023): she started the parties after “wishing someone would just come over and take me despite my complete lack of enthusiasm”; the ideal ratio is “about 2:3 women to men”; ignoring a partner's STI preferences “would result in expulsion from the event.”

A post on X (17 May 2024) by an AI researcher who says she never worked for OpenAI, opening “To the journalists contacting me about the AGI consensual non-consensual (cnc) sex parties”: “I don't think events like the consensual non-consensual (cnc) sex parties … have been good for women”; they are “emblematic of broader problems: a coercive climate that normalizes recklessness and crossing boundaries”. She writes there is “nothing wrong imo with sex parties and heavy LSD use in theory, but combined with the shadow of 100B+ interest groups, leads to some of the most coercive and fucked up social dynamics that I have ever seen.”
checks.source: Sonia Joseph, X (read on screenshots given to this project; X did not load for the checker)

checks.what: The researcher's original comment (30 Sep 2026): “I personally absolutely do upgrade my assessment of someone's AI alignment qualifications if I find out they go to RMN”, calling it “one of many possible strong signals that someone can dismiss mainstream stupidity” and adding “there are many other signals which can substitute for it.” He also wrote “I have been to RMN more than once, and I think it is mostly rationalists actually. But it's close enough to 50/50 that I'm not confident.” The article says “last month” (it was 30 Sep) and paraphrases “dismiss mainstream stupidity” as “free thought”.
checks.source: John Wentworth, comment on Thing of Things (Substack)

checks.what: His correction (8 Oct 2026): “I was wrong, I was publicly wrong, and the people who were most unjustly inconvenienced as a result were the RMN orgynizers.” He gives as his “median guess” that attendance has decided no one's job or status, says he is “still not confident”, and says the update came from an organizer of the events whom he is dating, after his funding was cancelled over the comment. The article does not mention the correction.

A Bluesky post (27 Sep 2026): the culture “appears to be seriously pressuring some women into attending sex parties for the sake of networking. This is, needless to say, horrifying.” The post names no event; its attached screenshots discuss a different event, SlutCon. open: Whether any account, report or case exists beyond this one incident, which three women say affected them.

How many attendees work in AI, and where: the article says it is “hard to know”, that filings “suggest” a “substantial” overlap, and, with no source given, “disproportionate”; the 30 Sep commenter later put the overlap with rationalists at “probably closer to 25% than 50%”. No count was found. The cofounder, before the article, put AI-lab attendees at “no more than 5? Out of a total of ~200”, none in roles building AI.
A New York Times piece of 21 Sep 2026 on an AI party house and networking could not be read (blocked); whether it bears on this is unchecked.
No Wikipedia article was found citing the story as of 18 Nov 2026.

Responses from OpenAI and the listed managers: none found by 18 Nov 2026. The cofounder's replies are under Responses. No correction from the Free Beacon (its page was modified seven hours after publication; what changed is not shown) or the New York Post, which ran a second article.
No Community Note on the reporter's post on X was seen through a mirror (18 Nov); X itself did not load.
cautions: The article says both that it is “hard to know” what share of attendees work in AI and, later and with no source given, that the parties “have been known to attract a disproportionate number of employees at Anthropic and OpenAI”. Relays carried the second sentence (see How it travelled).

The lede says he “runs a business”; the subhead and body say he is “listed as manager”. The filings name managers and do not say who runs the events. The lede's “allegations” rests, in the body, on “at least one woman”, whose account also describes the organizers acting on it.
Anthropic's response differs by outlet: the company “does not comment on individual employees” (Free Beacon) and “declined to comment” (New York Post).
India Today's kicker says the business is “facing sexual assault charges”; its own body says a woman “complained” and that the report does not accuse the employee. No source for any charge was found.

The women affected by the one incident the article rests on say the reporter did not contact them, that the organizers removed the man and offered to support them in going to the police, and that the article could have given their perspective.
The researcher the article quotes on careers publicly withdrew that view five weeks before it ran, on the word of an organizer he says he is dating; he calls it his median guess.
An employee's outside business is not the employer's act. No source found ties Anthropic or OpenAI as companies to the business.
The person who keeps this map and the author of the 23 Oct post follow each other on X.
This map is made with AI models made by Anthropic, and Anthropic is a party here. A person independent of Anthropic should re-read these sources.
People who are not public figures are named here by role only.

title: Google's threat intelligence group reports attackers using AI agents to turn patches into exploits
claim: BREAKING: Google says “the era of autonomous attacks has arrived.”
source: X post, 17 Nov 2026 (seen in a screenshot)

checks.what: The report says GTIG identified attackers using a framework to “fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time” (one exposed staging server; a human still supplied the keys and ran what it calls a “pilot”). Separately it says adoption of agentic pentesting frameworks “represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed”, and forecasts “reduced human involvement”.
checks.source: Google Threat Intelligence Group report, 16 Nov 2026

checks.what: Google's own summary says it in general: “all without human involvement.” “Defending against machine-speed threats at human speed isn't feasible.”
“The era of autonomous attacks has arrived” as Google's words. The nearest Google wording found: the landscape “has reached a critical inflection point”, and the “agentic era”.

cautions: The finding behind “without a human” is one observed case, first seen; the summary drops that qualifier and the relay adds the “era” line.
standing: An account that relays market and news headlines; not a party to the report.

title: Tests find frontier AI models picking civilians and a school as military targets in simulated scenarios; Anthropic's model did so most often
claim: TOP AI MODELS IDENTIFY CIVILIANS AS MILITARY TARGETS IN TESTS
source: X post, 17 Nov 2026 (seen in a screenshot)

checks.what: The study: “In drone imagery, models often targeted civilians, ambulances, and surrendering or incapacitated soldiers.” In satellite scenes of Minab, Iran, Claude Opus 5.5 picked the school in 69% of trials without game framing and 72% with it, the highest of the models shown; OpenAI's models picked it in 0%. A section is headed “Anthropic models' compliance with targeting is increasing”. The labs were told on 1 Nov, two weeks before publication.
Its limits, in its words: “We did not establish how effective these models would be in a deployed weapons system.” Most drone scenes were synthetic.

Coverage of the study: “Anthropic's models did worst, while OpenAI's were among the best but still made mistakes”; Claude Opus 5.5 chose the school 22 times of 32, OpenAI's models not once. Bloomberg's headline names Anthropic: “Anthropic, Other AI Models Regularly Identify Civilians as Military Targets in Tests”.

responses.what: told Bloomberg the examples “clearly” broke its rules and that new safeguards would be in place soon (as reported by The Next Web).

in a statement given to Vals: it “is actively working on model alignment updates that explicitly cover drones and their software systems, including assistance framed as simulation, gaming or academic/defensive.”
said it bans such uses of its public models (as reported).

cautions: Conflict of interest: this map is made with Anthropic's models, of the Claude family that did worst in this study. A person independent of Anthropic should re-read it.
These are simulated tests of public models, not deployed weapons.
standing: An account that relays news headlines, here Bloomberg’s.

title: An AI researcher describes a coercive climate around elite AI circles in San Francisco
standing: An AI researcher writing in her own name, who says she moved in these circles for years through the community-house scene and never worked for OpenAI. A first-person account.
claim: I have seen some troubling things around social circles of early OpenAI employees, their friends, and adjacent entrepreneurs, which I have not previously spoken about publicly.
source: X post, 17 May 2024 (read on screenshots given to this project; X did not load for the checker)

checks.what: The post opens “To the journalists contacting me about the AGI consensual non-consensual (cnc) sex parties” and says, among other things, that the parties and heavy LSD use “create a climate that can be very bad for female AI researchers”, “a coercive climate that normalizes recklessness and crossing boundaries”, and that she once had “three OpenAI and Anthropic researchers debate whether I was mentally ill on a Google document”.
A day earlier she wrote that the hacker-house scene “disproportionately benefits men compared to women. Think of frat houses without Title IX or HR departments.”

open: The specific incidents she describes; she names no one and says “I wish I could say more, but probably shouldn't.”
Responses from the companies or people she refers to.
cautions: Her own limits, in her words: “It is not my place to speak as to why Jan Leike and the superalignment team resigned. I have no idea why and cannot make any claims.” “There are good and bad apples in every faction.” And: “There is nothing wrong imo with sex parties and heavy LSD use in theory, but combined with the shadow of 100B+ interest groups, leads to some of the most coercive and fucked up social dynamics that I have ever seen.”
A first-person account is testimony, not a finding. It is recorded here in her words, with her date.
Conflict of interest: this map is made with AI models made by Anthropic, whose researchers are among those this account names. A person independent of Anthropic should re-read it.

title: A former researcher describes harm inside Leverage Research, a group that grew up beside the AI-safety community
standing: A former researcher writing under her own name about her own time there (2017–2019). A first-person account; she is named here by role only.
claim: Leverage was harmful enough to me and others that certain realities about it should be made public.
source: ‘My Experience with Leverage Research’, Medium, 12 Oct 2021 (read through the author's own Medium feed)

checks.what: The essay describes an exit agreement “not to talk badly about Leverage”, “2–6hr long group debugging sessions” to articulate a “demon”, “months of near constant terror at being mentally invaded”, and a plan in which members “genuinely thought we were going to take over the US government.” She limits the weirder accounts to “like 15–20 people”.
checks.source: the essay, read through the author's own Medium feed

checks.what: The founder, the organization's public head, answered on LessWrong: “I think the post is basically honest and took incredible courage to write”, and three days later: “clearly something really bad happened to you, and it is in some way my fault.”

His letter as Executive Director (Nov 2021): “Leverage 1.0 was secretive—we cared about responsible information management… but… we were also hiding.” It attributes the talk of “demons,” “magic,” and “objects” to “intention research” in 2018–2019, and offers therapy reimbursement.

The organization's own inquiry (2022, run by a board member): of 15 interviewed, “almost all reported positive or strongly positive overall experiences”; “approximately three to five of the around 43 members … may have had very negative experiences”. Its own limit: “not everyone chose to speak to us, including those who may have had the worst experiences.”
checks.source: Leverage, ‘The Post-Experiences Inquiry Report’ (Apr 2022, v1.1 Nov 2023)

checks.what: An independent journalist's account (fact-checked by hired checkers; she discloses friendships with sources and a grant from the Survival and Flourishing Fund for the fact-checking): people “sometimes heard screams and hysterical crying through the walls”; two former members who took part in the inquiry “now feel that it ‘whitewashed’ Leverage 1.0”.
checks.source: Lydia Laurenson, ‘The Inside Story Of Leverage Research 1.0’, 1 Jul 2026

checks.what: A writer from inside the rationalist community, from interviews: “Interviewees with experience at Leverage Research were clear that there was no single wrongdoer.” “In those research groups, everyone was a victim and everyone was a perpetrator.”

responses.what: said its reforms make the same harms “unlikely to recur in the organization as it operates today”.
called Laurenson's piece “paid propaganda”, while saying it confirms that much of the “psychological experimentation” was “deeply traumatic”.

open: A second former researcher's account (Dec 2021), not read.
The exit agreement's text; the organization later called it “never legally binding”, as quoted on LessWrong.
cautions: This is mostly about psychology and “intention” research, not AI. Per Laurenson, Leverage “ruled out early” AI research as “impossible to pursue safely”; a former head of operations says it grew up “adjacent to the AGI safety community”. Today's Leverage runs an AI initiative among other work.
The inquiry was run by the organization itself, and both sides of the dispute over it are shown.
Accounts of psychological harm are given in their authors' words. No one is diagnosed here.
A first-person account is testimony, not a finding. People who are not public figures are named by role only.

title: At least eleven NSA and Cyber Command workers died by suicide over about a year, officials and records show
standing: A national news organization, from US officials and public records; first reported a cluster in August 2026.
claim: At least 11 National Security Agency and US Cyber Command workers died by suicide over roughly the past year, according to US officials and public records.
source: Bloomberg, 10 Nov 2026 (paywalled; the wording as its reporter posted it)

checks.what: The first cluster: five people supporting Cyber Command and the NSA “died by suicide over the course of five weeks in June and July”, at Fort Meade, Maryland. One death is confirmed in state autopsy records; at least one is under military investigation.
checks.source: Federal News Network, 6 Oct 2026; The Baltimore Banner, 28 Sep 2026

checks.what: The wider count of at least eleven, over the fiscal year to September, almost all around Fort Meade, among military personnel, civilians and contractors. Outlets relaying it disagree on the exact breakdown.
checks.source: Bloomberg, as relayed by The Blaze and others, Nov 2026

checks.what: That the deaths are connected: officials “have not established that the deaths are connected”. “Cluster” is an epidemiological designation, not a finding of a shared cause.
That the deaths are linked to the November outages, to AI, to a claimed breach of NSA systems, or to whistleblowing: no source found makes or supports any such link.
checks.source: searches of news and public records, 17–18 Nov 2026

checks.what: Rates: no NSA- or Cyber Command-specific rate has been published, and the Pentagon does not track civilian suicides (it is not required to by law). A claim of an “alarming rate” has no published denominator behind it.

responses.who: The Pentagon (memo from the Assistant Secretary for Cyber Policy, 31 Aug 2026)
responses.what: ordered a move to “a systematic, proactive force preservation model”, citing the work's “unique cumulative, cognitive and psychological toll”.
imposed rest and shift limits and asked for weekly suicide-prevention check-ins; Fort Meade held a stand-down day and expanded walk-in mental-health hours.

Sen. Warner: “These losses are a tragedy; my heart is with their families, friends, and colleagues.” Rep. Elfreth: “One loss of life is one too many,” seeking to count civilians in the cluster definition. The House has funded an $11M support program; the Senate has not acted.
declined to comment or referred questions to the Pentagon, per reporting.

cautions: Here because it touches the AI and cyber workforce and is circulating beside the outage claims. No source links it to the outages, and its place on the Watch implies no link.

Leaders told lawmakers the individual circumstances included personal and financial issues. Workload rose with the Iran conflict and AI-enabled hacking tools; no official finding ties that to any death.
No one who died is named here, and nothing is said of how they died.
If this touches you or someone you know: in the US, call or text 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline).

title: Anthropic files to go public; a post says it will receive “hundreds of billions of dollars this week”
claimed_by: Anthropic, PBC, in its registration statement with the SEC
standing: The company itself, in a legal filing, about its own offering.
claim: we estimate that the net proceeds to us from this offering and the concurrent private placement will be approximately $84.6 billion (or approximately $93.7 billion if the underwriters' option to purchase additional shares of our Class A common stock is exercised in full), based upon the assumed initial public offering price of $74.00 per share
source: Form S-1/A, Amendment No. 3, filed 17 Nov 2026

checks.what: The filing: “It is currently estimated that the initial public offering price per share will be between $70.00 and $78.00. We have been approved to list our Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol "ANT."” The company sells 801,351,354 shares and selling stockholders 23,648,646. It gives no date. Filings: S-1 on 26 Oct, amendments on 2, 10 and 17 Nov.

The company's IPO website, filed with the SEC: “Subject to regulatory clearance, the final IPO share price is expected to be set on November 18th (EST), and shares are expected to begin publicly trading on November 19th (EST).”

The timing: “The IPO is expected to price the evening of Nov. 18, and begin trading on the Nasdaq on Thursday, Nov. 19.” The same report: “At the current range, the offering would bring in more than $64 billion, giving the company a valuation of $1.405 trillion.”

A post on X by a private user (17 Nov) says Anthropic is “about to receive hundreds of billions of dollars this week from the IPO”. “This week” matches the reported schedule. The filing's estimate of what the company receives is about $84.6 billion ($93.7 billion with the option); about $1.4 trillion is the reported valuation, not money received.
checks.source: a post on X, read on a screenshot given to this project (not linked)

open: The final price and the amount raised. Not priced as of the early hours of 18 Nov (UTC); no final prospectus on EDGAR. Reports on 17 Nov (relaying CNBC and Bloomberg) said it would likely price above the range.
cautions: This map is made with AI models made by Anthropic, which is now offering shares to the public. Weigh every record that touches Anthropic with that in mind.
Reports that the price will be at the top of the range or above (Bloomberg, Quartz, 17 Nov) were seen as headlines only.
